rv.q: Taylor Mac's 'Gary: A Sequel to Titus Andronicus' is a brilliant, blood-soaked comedy that finds profound meaning in the aftermath of Shakespeare's goriest tragedy.

"An outrageous mix of the absurd and the grotesque, designed to make audiences gape...Lane is tremendous, and Julie White is screamingly funny as the play’s third character, Carol...While George C. Wolfe’s production delivers all the flatulence a person could desire, there are stretches where it runs out of gas...
Never has that been clearer than in “Gary,” as important and risky a role that he ever has assumed.
The play is genuinely funny, and not just because it's absurd.
Even if the blood is obviously fake and the corpses cartoons, it is hard to keep both your sense of humor and horror engaged at once.
There's no shortage of art and craft in this offbeat show; but there's also a limit to how much goofiness a comedy can support, and Mac may have gone over his limit.

I have never liked Lane and White as wholeheartedly as I did watching them in “Gary: A Sequel to Titus Andronicus,” mostly because of their and Neilsen’s admiration for the script, and where it takes them as performers.
And it feels like some of these things, some of the time.
Taylor Mac may have a message, but it gets lost in humor fit mostly for teenage boys.
Unfortunately, despite the tremendous abundance of talent both onstage and off, the production is mainly notable for being the most batshit-crazy thing to be seen on Broadway in many a moon.
An inspired idea, a comedic follow-up to Shakespeare’s brutal tragedy, is sadly not enough to sustain a disappointingly thin show
Though ambitious, it’s neither funny enough nor tragic enough; it’s also frequently hard to follow.
What Mac offers us instead is an exercise in self-indulgence, with a dollop of facile allusion and a dose of bad faith.
Gary, too, is a welcome sign of new life, the work of a truly sui generis talent who, if we’re lucky, will be blessing Broadway—as a performer, too, hopefully—for years to come.
"An eccentric combination of high-brow references and low-brow laughs that has something to offend everyone, a whole lot to provoke thought, and a refreshingly uplifting moral...

"No one knows how to create a beautiful mess quite like creative genius Taylor Mac...Weird, sexy, uncomfortable romp...The blood and piss and flatulence and other bodily excretions that can’t be ignored are on full display. And Mac manages to make a joyful playpen of weirdness from all the realities often considered shameful...
For the rest of us, it’s clear that Charles Ludlam is smiling down on Broadway and laughing his head off this Easter Sunday.
In Gary, his characters succeed.
Its presence in this season thrillingly asserts that Broadway can still be a home for challenging new American plays.
This is bold, audacious work -- Broadway has not seen anything quite like this before.
Those who relish low comedy will have a ball as do the actors on stage.
Gary is a farce, a piece of messy circus whose many tones and shades will likely divide audiences and critics.

...while the philosophical issues of leadership, class and art don't always land as completely as the expertly-performed wordplay and slapstick, not to mention a rousing spectacle near the finish that is best left as a surprise, Gary: A Sequel to Titus Andronicus is bound inspire further thought about those who create madness in art to inspire r...
Gary is a comic concoction that will hit home with some theatergoers but make many wince, especially at the excessive use of low comedy and bloody stage business.

When Mac starts to think too hard, though, it falters a bit.
What emerges often tastes simultaneously overbaked and undercooked.
In the end we have no idea what we have watched or why.
It’s been said that comedy is tragedy plus time.
Mac’s dexterity in weaving such social indictments into a madcap comedy rife with fart gags and dick jokes is a wonder to witness.
Wildly funny and clever, this play by Taylor Mac, directed by George C. Wolfe is one a serious theater-goer cannot miss.
It’s dastardly delicious in its absurdity, craftily crazed but hard to dig deep in that shallow end of the pure waters of brilliant nonsense.
It is messy as hell and an indisputable work of genius.
Unfortunately the proceedings occasionally get bogged down like a battalion tramping through a muddy quagmire.
If the whole isn’t greater than the sum of its parts, Hadestown still has effective elements that come together for the best atmosphere on Broadway.

"Taylor Mac is known for extravagant and experimental work, and if that is what you are looking for, 'Gary' does not disappoint. But if you are coming for composure and coherence, this is likely not the show for you. Much like the dining room of corpses, this play feels a bit overstuffed.
Wolfe gives the actors free rein to pull out all the stops and go for yocks with every line delivery and reaction, but even these master farceurs struggle to keep the fun funny for 95 minutes.
But Taylor Mac’s “Gary: A Sequel to Titus Andronicus” is utter crap.
Gary: A Sequel to Titus Andronicus, is the wildest ride on Broadway this season—unhinged, harrowing and hilarious.
This political satire is stroked with double entendres that are hit or miss.
Other than being a star vehicle for Nathan Lane, why is Gary even on Broadway?

cn.t: Critics are divided on Taylor Mac's audacious Broadway debut: some praise its wild humor and political urgency, while others find it a labored, scatological mess that wastes a stellar cast of Nathan Lane, Kristine Nielsen, and Julie White.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.
